newsitem.title: FRANCE: French PM raps Socialists, rightists start poll bid.
newsitem.headline: French PM raps Socialists, rightists start poll bid.

text.p: Prime Minister Alain Juppe said on Thursday French voters faced a choice between lasting economic growth with the present centre-right government and an "artificial boost" with the Socialists.

As the far-right National Front also launched its bid for a toehold in parliament in snap elections called for May 25 and June 1, the Gaullist premier told a party conference voters must chose between "a society in which people participate and a society where regulation rules."
"The choice is between an artificial boost and lasting economic growth," Juppe said. The opposition Socialists have said they would seek to stimulate consumer demand to engineer faster growth.
Juppe's audience included only a few of the heavyweights in the fractious centre-right bloc, including former prime minister Edouard Balladur.
Both National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin and former interior minister Charles Pasqua, outspoken critics of Juppe, stayed away.

"The Socialists want to eradicate unemployment by creating jobs with decrees. They regulate from above...We need to rebuild the confidence of the new generations in employment," said Juppe, whose popularity has slumped as unemployment has risen from 11.7 percent when he took office in 1995 to a record 12.8 percent.
At a May Day parade through the heart of Paris, far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen and his National Front launched their campaign.

Le Pen's traditional May Day festival, honouring French mediaeval hero Joan of Arc who drove the English out of France, was broadened this year to advance the Front's bid for seats in the National Assembly, where it currently has none.
Some 10,000 party loyalists turned out for the demonstration in bright sunshine. Across the city leftist trade unions planned a labour march later in the day.

The Front, which wants to ship immigrants home and give a constitutional preference to "native-born French" in jobs and social benefits, has set a goal of 20 seats in parliamentary elections. Pollsters predict it will not win more than a handful.

Le Pen, who announced on the eve of the parade that he would not himself run in the election, has targeted the centre-right, saying the Front's priority was to "zap" it from power even if it meant a victory for the left.

A Le Pen supporter, an elderly woman who would not give her name, said he had made "just the right move" in deciding not to run. "He wants (President Jacques) Chirac to resign should he fail to win a majority, and Mr Le Pen wants to be available to launch his presidential campaign immediately," she said.
Several of France's main trade union leaders, divided on cuts in working hours and other employment issues, bowed out of the leftist May Day rally planned in Paris.

Marc Blondel, leader of the non-partisan Force Ouvriere, staged a rally in Bordeaux, in south-west France, where Juppe is mayor, and told reporters: "I don't want to give pulic opinion the idea that we are all agreed".
